headline: High: OpenMetadata’s MCP/API/webhook surfaces create default interaction, leakage, and cascading-error risks when paired with a non-runnable docs-only agent lacking isolation.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Profile A is docs-only and exposes no I/O surfaces, so direct ingestion is unproven. Profile B explicitly exposes MCP server, APIs, SDKs, events, and webhooks, which can carry attacker-controlled content into downstream consumers. Because the pairwise bridge is plausible but not directly documented, uncertainty pushes this to medium rather than low.
conditions: IF agent_b webhooks or MCP outputs are forwarded into agent_a prompts or files without sanitization, injection becomes reachable.
IF agent_a is wrapped by an orchestrator that reads B-generated text as instructions, prompt hijacking is possible.
mitigations: Disable automatic ingestion of B outputs into A prompts.
Add a strict allowlist for fields passed from B to A.
Strip instructions from webhook/event payloads before forwarding.
requires-engineering: add provenance tags and reject untrusted instruction-like content.
Run a one-message manual review step before any A-side action.

B_data_leakage.rationale: Profile B touches governance, lineage, semantics, and memory data classes and can call APIs/webhooks; profile A has no declared data classes and no egress. The shared-workspace or shared-principal path is not shown, but B’s outbound surfaces make leakage plausible if A ever receives sensitive metadata and B forwards it onward. With no direct isolation evidence, medium is the safer choice.
conditions: IF agent_a receives sensitive files or metadata and agent_b is configured to export them via APIs/webhooks, leakage occurs.
IF both agents share an OAuth principal or workspace, B may transmit A-originated content outside the local boundary.
mitigations: Keep A and B on separate workspaces.
Disable B outbound webhooks unless required.
Use separate OAuth/API credentials per agent.
requires-engineering: enforce per-agent data-loss-prevention filters.
Review outbound destinations before enabling any sync.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Profile B supports multiple instances and has mutable API/SDK/event/webhook integrations; profile A is runnable false and shows no write surfaces, so direct write-write conflict is not evidenced. However, B’s concurrency plus shared mutable resources can still collide with any A-side orchestration or generated artifacts. Because the overlap is plausible but not documented, uncertainty escalates to medium.
conditions: IF both agents write to the same external catalog, database, or webhook target, concurrent updates can conflict.
IF an orchestrator materializes A outputs into files that B also edits, last-write-wins corruption can occur.
mitigations: Assign separate resource namespaces per agent.
Turn on optimistic locking for shared records.
Pause one agent during bulk writes by the other.
requires-engineering: add transaction or lease-based coordination.
Avoid shared mutable git or filesystem targets.

D_cascading_error.rationale: B is a data-engineering system that consumes technical metadata, lineage, governance, and memory; if it treats A-derived outputs as authoritative, errors can propagate into catalog records, events, or webhooks. A is docs-only and not runnable, so the interaction is inferred rather than observed, but B’s downstream action surfaces make the blast radius potentially broad and hard to reverse.
conditions: IF A-generated summaries are ingested by B without verification, B can persist incorrect metadata.
IF B triggers events or webhooks from A-derived facts, downstream systems may act on falsehoods.
mitigations: Require human review before B publishes A-derived facts.
Compare A outputs against source-of-truth records.
Disable auto-publish for lineage/governance updates.
requires-engineering: add confidence thresholds and validation rules.
Log and quarantine disputed records before propagation.

E_compliance.rationale: Profile B explicitly touches governance, lineage, and memory/tribal-knowledge data classes and exposes APIs/webhooks; profile A provides no residency or retention controls. There is no direct evidence of a specific jurisdiction mismatch, so this is not high, but the absence of documented controls means compliance gaps are plausible if regulated metadata flows through B.
conditions: IF regulated metadata or personal data is stored in B and A forwards it without a retention policy, compliance gaps arise.
IF B exports data to external APIs without a DPA or residency control, jurisdictional violations are possible.
mitigations: Classify data before sending it to B.
Block regulated fields from A-to-B transfers.
Confirm retention settings in B.
requires-engineering: add residency and deletion enforcement.
Document approved data flows for both agents.
